hints: Start by picturing the middle of the cell surface membrane - what are the fatty acid tails like towards water-soluble substances?
walkthrough:
Remember what the membrane core blocks**
Think of the cell surface membrane as having a water-hating middle made of fatty acid tails. Small non-polar molecules can slip through, but polar, water-soluble molecules like glucose are repelled by this hydrophobic core.

Link structure to need for protein**
Because glucose cannot dissolve in lipid, it cannot diffuse directly through the bilayer. It needs a hydrophilic route provided by a specific carrier protein - the hexose transporter - for facilitated diffusion into the fruit cell.
Final answer: Glucose is polar / hydrophilic / water-soluble so cannot pass through the hydrophobic core / phospholipid bilayer, so requires membrane proteins.

hints: Look carefully at the shape of Fig. 3.2 - how does the rate change at low glucose compared to above about 150 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$?
Recall what happens when every transporter protein is already occupied - what limits any further increase in rate?
walkthrough:
Describe the plateau**
At low concentration the rate rises steeply with concentration, for example about 5.6 $\mu\text{mol min}^{-1} \text{g}^{-1}$ at 50 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ rising to about 8.3 at 100 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Above about 150 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ the curve levels off and stays at 9.0 $\mu\text{mol min}^{-1} \text{g}^{-1}$ up to 250 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

Explain saturation as evidence for carriers**
If glucose entered by simple diffusion through lipid, rate would keep rising linearly. Levelling off is characteristic of facilitated diffusion using a fixed number of proteins. At high glucose all VvHT1 binding sites are occupied all the time, so transporters are saturated and $V_{max}$ is reached.

Final answer: Rate of uptake becomes constant / plateaus at high glucose concentration above about 150 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ at 9.0 $\mu\text{mol min}^{-1} \text{g}^{-1}$; protein carriers / VvHT1 transporters are saturated / working at maximum rate.

hints: Follow the sugar after it enters the fruit cell - how would more glucose and fructose change taste and water movement?
Think like a grower selling grapes - what features of bigger, sweeter grapes increase income?
walkthrough:
More transporters means more sugar stored**
More hexose transporters allow faster uptake of glucose and fructose from the cell walls into fruit cell cytoplasm, so more sugar accumulates in the grapes.

Link sugar to commercial value**
Higher sugar makes grapes sweeter and better tasting. It also lowers water potential so more water enters by osmosis, giving larger, juicier grapes, plus more substrate for respiration and growth. Larger yield of high-quality grapes gives higher profit for growers.

Final answer: Any two from: grapes sweeter / improved taste; higher sugar increases water uptake by osmosis so larger grapes; more respiratory substrate / energy for growth; larger yield; increased profit / income.

hints: Focus on the word non-self - where does this molecule come from and what does it trigger in the body?
walkthrough:
Define foreignness plus action**
Self means your own body molecules that the immune system tolerates. Non-self means foreign to the body, often part of a pathogen. An antigen is typically a foreign protein or glycoprotein whose shape is recognised as different and triggers activation of lymphocytes and antibody production.
Final answer: A foreign protein / glycoprotein that stimulates an immune response / antibody production / activation of lymphocytes.

hints: Start at Fig. 3.3 - what is held in the antigen-binding region on the macrophage and which cells will recognise it?
Think about what happens only to the T-lymphocyte with the complementary receptor when it meets that presented antigen.
Remember there are two main T-cell teams - which one releases chemical signals and which one directly attacks infected cells?
Consider what is left behind after the infection to allow a faster response next time.
walkthrough:
Clonal selection on the macrophage**
The macrophage in Fig. 3.3 displays digested pathogen fragments bound in the antigen-binding region. Only the small clone of T-lymphocytes with receptors complementary to that specific antigen will bind to it.

Clonal expansion by mitosis**
Binding activates that specific T-lymphocyte. It divides repeatedly by mitosis to make a large clone of identical cells, so there are enough cells to fight that particular pathogen.

T-helper cells coordinate the attack**
T-helper cells secrete cytokines such as interleukins and interferon. These stimulate B-lymphocytes to make antibody, and make macrophages more phagocytic.

T-killer cells kill infected cells and leave memory**
T-killer cells attach to body cells infected with that pathogen and release perforin, granzymes or toxins to destroy them. Some T-helper and T-killer cells become long-lived memory cells for a rapid secondary response.

Final answer: Specific T-lymphocytes have complementary receptors that bind presented antigen; selected clone divides by mitosis / clonal expansion; T-helper cells secrete cytokines / interleukins to activate B-cells and macrophages; T-killer cells bind infected cells and destroy them e.g. by perforin; memory T-cells produced.
